extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, and workshop participants (comedy/theatre)
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises and principles for building improv scenes: creating physical/mental platforms, using status-transfers and coaching techniques, breaking routines, and teaching performers to make offers and define relationships quickly. Includes step-by-step games and coaching notes for workshop leaders and students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status (transfer status by giving improviser's thoughts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the improviser their real thoughts (e.g., tell them what Andrew Willson would be thinking) so they automatically know what to say and don't need lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alexandra coaching Claire by saying Alex’s thoughts; James as Ed told to be 'very tired but enthusiastic'. Benefits: the thoughts are obvious and human, generate authentic, hilarious responses, free improvisers from planning, and create audience recognition ('we all think but never say this'). Note dichotomy between what people think and what they ask improvisers to show—use this contrast for comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train performers to be someone else (role-coaching from the seat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Train improvisers to play another person's character by giving frequent direction from the coach's seat (hand signals, verbal cues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once trained, improvisers only need direction when they encounter unfamiliar situations. Example: Malcolm trained Ece to be him with frequent direction; Joanna/Claire exercise where one gives 'thoughts' and the other performs. Use this to let performers be in scene without constant external feeding, and allow occasional on-seat prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build platforms (use physical environment to generate story, character, comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a clear platform (physical set and specific offers) so the environment feeds story and character rather than leaving actors to gossip or talk about unrelated events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up simple furniture to suggest a living room; use the platform to inspire concrete actions and discoveries (objects, relationships). Emphasize that improv has an 'unlimited budget'—if you commit to a setting the audience will believe it. Platforms should enlighten character (ownership, backstory) so the environment feeds the scene rather than remaining decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go through an unusual door / let the hand decide
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the instruction 'go through an unusual door' and have performers 'let the hand decide'—reach out and let an instinctive gesture determine what is behind the door.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique avoids planning: 'Whatever is in your head, keep it there... at the last moment you’re going to do something else and surprise yourself' (Patti Stiles). Use the door to create an immediate, defining platform (e.g., high-tech flat, palatial interior) and encourage performers to show rather than tell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start positive
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin scenes/activities from a positive stance as an instruction to improvisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an upfront reminder in exercises (e.g., when entering a flat). Starting positive helps actors commit to offers and keeps the scene forward-moving and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Everything-for-a-reason (establish causes and justify offers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience assumes every action/detail has a reason; causes must be established or the logic of the story collapses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a sticking door implies a run-down flat—if later location is palatial, the contradiction needs justification or audience faith is lost. Prefer reasons to follow actions; reinforce causes when possible. See related exercises (Master/Servant Dubbing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make promises and fulfill them (reincorporation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create promises/prominent offers in the platform and then fulfill or reincorporate them later to satisfy audience expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: remote-controlled lighting, robot factory, palm-print door leading to trapped guest. Audiences anticipate fulfillment; items reincorporated rarely need extra justification. Fill environment with potentially useful specifics and remember them to pick up later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making assumptions / blind offers as invitation to define
rubrics_metrics.description: Make blind offers (e.g., 'this looks a hundred years old') as invitations for the scene partners to define—provided the offerer will define if no one else does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching this skill prevents blind offers becoming 'wimping'. Encourage improvisers to be willing to contribute definitions and backstory so blind offers become productive rather than evasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Define relationships, objects and space early in the scene: 'If you define quickly enough you can’t be wrong.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delaying definitions risks contradiction later and confuses audience expectations. Encourage early, confident offers about relationship or space to free subsequent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name or use mime objects quickly (don’t ask 'What is it?')
rubrics_metrics.description: When handed a mime object, name or use it quickly rather than asking 'What is it?' which breaks reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If receiving a mime you should name any plausible object; if it doesn't quite fit, justify it. Asking 'What is it?' hands an awkward problem back to partner and makes the audience question the improviser's perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse Twenty Questions (exercise to illustrate need for shared definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Group chooses objects while guesser is out; guesser asks yes/no questions and group tries to maintain illusion of a single object—demonstrates how lack of shared definition creates impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this game to show how scenes fall apart when participants don't agree on definitions, or keep interacting with undefined objects/relationships. Good warm-up to illustrate consistent worldbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Up the absurdity curve (break routine gradually)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase absurdity progressively rather than jumping to extreme bizarre offers immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with small eccentricities and escalate (e.g., many locks on a door) so the audience enjoys the build. Immediate extreme absurdity often kills the scene or forces an even bigger idea to top it; instead, escalate and choose when to discard clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Alice (sane reactant) vs Mad Hatter (insane)
rubrics_metrics.description: Playing a sane character ('Alice') in an insane world generates story faster than everyone being bizarre ('Mad Hatter').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice reacting seriously to absurdity makes partners funnier and the show stronger. Coaches should discourage performers who always try to be the funny one and encourage reactive 'Alice' choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obsess on one object (use focus to develop story)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focusing on a single discovered object can sustain audience interest and be used to drive a break in routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of over-fixation early—if you get too invested you may run out of material when you need to move on. Use obsession judiciously or 'yes-and' one object to escalate toward a payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add an object that doesn't fit (create contrast to reveal character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce one item that contradicts the established theme to break routine and reveal character detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: squalid flat with a gleaming 42-inch TV signals the owner’s devotion to TV and creates richer character history. Use after the theme is established so the mismatch has impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a strong reaction (be changed emotionally)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine, strong emotional reaction creates the sense that 'something has happened' and propels the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusal to be changed is blocking. Strong reactions can be used as blind offers (e.g., 'Oh my god!')—partners must capitalize, escalate and reincorporate to create meaningful story and comedy. Connects to 'Being Changed' concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-coach timid improvisers / balance contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for timid students letting partners dominate; side-coach them to make offers and take part in defining the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage turn-taking in offers so one person doesn't control the platform. Use side-coaching to prompt quiet performers to contribute specifics and avoid 'wimping'.

rubrics_metrics.name: CJ sweep / create a rich visual world (scan the space)
rubrics_metrics.description: Train performers to 'sweep' the imagined space with their eyes and notice objects, smells, textures etc., so they 'see' an environment rather than inventing from scratch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises: one partner asks open questions ('Where are you? What can you smell?'); use side-coaching; have performers enter a space and then play a scene using as many environmental details as useful. The mental sweep supplies immediate, usable offers and makes performers look present in the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid planning; embrace last-moment spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourage pre-planning; use last-moment choices and outside direction to keep scenes lively and spontaneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: 'let the hand decide', external voices giving thoughts/direction, Patti Stiles' last-moment surprise. Experience shows outside direction often speeds action rather than slowing it and liberates improvisers to be imaginative, funny and physical.
